title: Errors are values
summary: Returned, not thrown. Wrapping, errors.Is and errors.As, and when a panic is right.

concepts.title: error is just an interface
concepts.brief:
There are no exceptions. `error` is an ordinary one-method interface —
`type error interface { Error() string }` — and failures are **returned** alongside results.

That is why Go code is full of `if err != nil`. The upside is that every failure path is visible in the source and the compiler makes you name the error; the cost is verbosity, which the language accepts on purpose.

The convention is firm: the error is the **last** return value, and when it is non-nil the other values are **not meaningful** unless the function documents otherwise — as `io.Reader` does, where `Read` can return both bytes and `io.EOF`.

examples.label: The shape of everything
examples.note: `err` last, checked immediately, wrapped with context on the way up. This four-line shape is most of the error handling you will ever write.

examples.label: Making one
examples.note: `%w` is the only one that preserves the original for `errors.Is` and `errors.As`. `%v` flattens it to text.

items.prompt: What makes a type usable as an `error`?
choices: Having a method `Error() string` — error is a normal one-method interface
Embedding the built-in `error` type
Being created by `errors.New` or `fmt.Errorf`
Implementing `String() string`
items.explain: One method, `Error() string`. `error` is predeclared but entirely ordinary, which is what lets you define a struct with fields, return it as an error, and recover the fields later with `errors.As`. Note it is `Error()`, not `String()` — implementing the wrong one is a quiet way to not be an error at all.

items.prompt: A function returns `(*User, error)` and the error is non-nil. What should you assume about the `*User`?
choices: Nothing — treat it as unusable unless the function documents otherwise
It is always nil when the error is non-nil
It holds whatever was parsed before the failure
It is the zero value, guaranteed by the compiler
items.explain: By convention the other values are meaningless on error, and nothing enforces it. Some functions deliberately return both — `Read` returns n bytes *and* `io.EOF`, and ignoring n there loses data. So: assume unusable, and check the documentation when it matters.

items.prompt: You wrap with `fmt.Errorf("load: %v", err)` instead of `%w`. What breaks?
choices: errors.Is and errors.As can no longer see the original error
Nothing — %v and %w produce the same error value
The message loses the original text
The error can no longer be compared with ==
items.explain: The message looks identical, which is what makes this hard to spot. But `%v` flattens the original to a string, so the chain is cut: `errors.Is(err, os.ErrNotExist)` starts returning false and a caller's retry logic silently stops working. Use `%w` unless you deliberately want to hide the cause.

items.prompt: Which standard-library function creates an error from a fixed string, with no formatting?
items.explain: `errors.New("...")`. Each call returns a **distinct** value even for identical text, so two separately-created errors with the same message are never `==`. That is exactly why sentinels are package-level variables created once, rather than built at the point of failure.

concepts.title: Wrapping, Is and As
concepts.brief:
`%w` wraps an error inside another, building a **chain** that keeps the original reachable while each layer adds context.

- `errors.Is(err, target)` — walks the chain looking for a specific **value**, like `os.ErrNotExist`. This is how you test for sentinels.
- `errors.As(err, &target)` — walks the chain looking for a specific **type**, and assigns it so you can read its fields.

Use these instead of `==` and a type assertion. The moment anything in the stack wraps, a direct comparison stops matching — and you will not find out until the layer that wraps is added months later.

examples.label: A chain, and reading through it
examples.code:
// three layers deep
err := fmt.Errorf("handle request: %w",
	fmt.Errorf("load config: %w", os.ErrNotExist))

err == os.ErrNotExist              // false - it is wrapped twice
errors.Is(err, os.ErrNotExist)     // true  - walks the chain

err.Error()
// handle request: load config: file does not exist
examples.note: Each layer prepends its context, so the message reads outermost-first and tells you the path through the code.

examples.label: Getting the details back
examples.note: `As` takes a **pointer to** the target variable, and panics if you forget the `&`. The target is set to the first matching error in the chain.

items.prompt: A helper wraps its error with `%w`. Your caller still tests `if err == os.ErrNotExist`.
choices: The comparison is now false; use errors.Is to walk the chain
It still works — == follows the wrap chain
It still works, but only one level deep
It does not compile once the error is wrapped
items.explain: `==` compares the outer value only, and the outer value is now the wrapper. `errors.Is` exists precisely so that adding context to an error somewhere in the middle of a call stack cannot silently break a caller's check. Reach for `errors.Is` by default.

items.prompt: You need the `ID` field off a `*NotFoundError` that is wrapped two layers deep. Which do you use?
choices: errors.As — it finds by type and assigns it so you can read fields
errors.Is — it finds by type and returns the match
A type assertion on err, after calling errors.Unwrap twice
errors.Join, then read the first element
items.explain: `As` is the type-based one and gives you the value; `Is` is the value-based one and gives you a bool. The mnemonic: **Is** this specific error? **As** this kind of error? Unwrapping by hand works but breaks when anyone changes the number of layers.

items.prompt: You call `errors.As(err, nf)` where `nf` is already a `*NotFoundError`, without the `&`.
choices: It panics — As requires a pointer to the target variable
It works; nf is already a pointer
It returns false silently
It does not compile
items.explain: `As` has to *assign* to your variable, so it needs the address of the variable itself — `&nf`, a `**NotFoundError`. Passing the wrong thing panics at runtime rather than failing to compile, because the parameter is an `any`. Always `var x *T; errors.As(err, &x)`.

items.prompt: Match each tool to what it is for.
pairs: Adds context while keeping the original reachable
Is this a specific error value, anywhere in the chain?
Is there an error of this type, and give it to me
items.explain: `errors.Join` arrived in Go 1.20 for the case where several things failed and you do not want to pick one — a batch, or several cleanup steps. `errors.Is` and `As` both see through a join as well as a wrap.

items.prompt: What is wrong with `if err != nil { return err }` at every layer?
choices: The final message has no path through the code — just "file does not exist"
It loses the wrap chain, so errors.Is stops working
It is slower, because the error is copied at every layer
Nothing; bare returns are the idiomatic form
items.explain: The chain survives — nothing is lost — but you end up at the top with `file does not exist` and no idea which file or which operation. Add context at each layer that knows something the one below does not: `fmt.Errorf("load user %d: %w", id, err)`. Do not repeat what the inner error already says.

concepts.title: Sentinels and custom types
concepts.brief:
Two ways to let a caller react to a *specific* failure:

- A **sentinel** — a package-level `var ErrNotFound = errors.New("not found")` that callers test with `errors.Is`. Simple, but it becomes part of your public API forever.
- A **custom type** — a struct with fields, found with `errors.As`. Use it when the caller needs *details*, not just the category.

The naming convention is strict enough to rely on: sentinel values start with `Err`, error types end in `Error`. `io.EOF` is the famous exception, and it is also the most important sentinel in the language — `Read` returns it to mean "nothing left", which is an expected outcome rather than a failure.

examples.label: Both forms
examples.note: Sentinels are created once at package level so identity comparison is stable; building one per failure would make `errors.Is` useless.

examples.label: io.EOF is not a failure
examples.note: `Read` may return bytes *and* `io.EOF` in the same call. Checking the error before using `n` is a real and easy way to drop the last chunk of a file.

items.prompt: Callers need to know which field failed validation, not just that validation failed. Sentinel or custom type?
choices: A custom type with a Field, retrieved with errors.As
A sentinel per field, tested with errors.Is
A sentinel, with the field name formatted into the message
Return a plain string alongside the error
items.explain: Details mean a type. A sentinel only answers yes/no, and parsing the field back out of the message is the kind of thing that works until someone rewords it. Rule of thumb: sentinel for a category the caller branches on, type when they need data.

items.prompt: Put one iteration of a correct Read loop in order.
steps: Call Read into the buffer, getting n and err
If n > 0, process buf[:n] — bytes can arrive alongside an error
If err is io.EOF, stop: this is the normal end of the stream
If err is any other non-nil, return it as a real failure
items.explain: Processing before checking the error is the part people get wrong, and it silently truncates the last read. The `io` documentation is explicit that callers should handle the bytes returned before considering the error. Most code avoids this by using `io.ReadAll` or `bufio.Scanner` instead of calling `Read` directly.

items.prompt: Match each name to what it is, by convention.
pairs: A sentinel value, compared with errors.Is
An error type, found with errors.As
A sentinel meaning the stream ended normally
The function that makes a sentinel
items.explain: The `Err` prefix versus the `Error` suffix is a reliable signal in someone else's package: it tells you whether to reach for `Is` or `As` before you read any documentation.

items.prompt: What is the main cost of exporting a sentinel like `ErrNotFound`?
choices: It is public API — callers depend on it, so it cannot be removed or re-meant
It allocates on every comparison
It cannot be wrapped with %w
It prevents the package from defining error types as well
items.explain: Once it is exported, someone's retry logic is keyed on it and removing it is a breaking change. That is the argument for keeping sentinels few and deliberate, and for not exporting one until a caller actually needs to branch on it.

concepts.title: When a panic is the right answer
concepts.brief:
A panic is for a **bug**, not for a condition. The line: if a competent caller could have prevented it, it is a bug; if it depends on the world — a file, a network, user input — it is an error and must be returned.

The standard library is consistent about this. `strconv.Atoi("abc")` returns an error, because bad input is expected. Indexing past the end of a slice panics, because that is always a mistake in your code.

Panicking across a package boundary is close to always wrong. The exceptions are a failed invariant during initialization — `regexp.MustCompile`, `template.Must` — where the input is a constant in your source, so a failure means the program should never have started.

examples.label: The Must convention
examples.note: A `Must` prefix is a promise that it panics. Use them only where the input is fixed at compile time.

items.prompt: Which of these should return an error rather than panic?
choices: A config file is missing on disk
A user submits a malformed date
An index is past the end of a slice
A database connection times out
items.explain: Everything that depends on the world outside your process. The slice index is the odd one out: no input makes it correct, so it is a bug in your code and the runtime is right to stop you. Ask "could the caller have prevented this?" — if yes, panic; if no, return.

items.prompt: What does the `Must` prefix promise, as in `regexp.MustCompile`?
choices: It panics instead of returning an error, so use it only on fixed input
It retries until it succeeds
It is the thread-safe variant
It validates eagerly instead of lazily
items.explain: It panics on failure. That is acceptable at package level, where the argument is a literal and a failure means the binary is broken and should not start. Using `MustCompile` on a pattern that came from config turns a config typo into a crash loop.

items.prompt: A library you import panics on malformed input instead of returning an error. Why is that a problem beyond style?
choices: A panic unwinds past every caller, so it is not recoverable where the decision belongs
Panics cannot cross package boundaries at all
It prevents the caller from using defer
It forces the caller to run with -race
items.explain: The caller has the context to decide whether bad input is fatal, and a panic takes that away — their only defense is a `recover`, which is clumsy and has to sit in exactly the right goroutine. Returning an error leaves the decision with the code that can actually make it.

items.prompt: `strconv.Atoi("abc")` returns an error, but `s[10]` on a 3-element slice panics. What is the principle?
choices: Bad external input is an expected condition; a bad index is always a bug
Standard library functions never panic, only the runtime does
Conversions return errors; operators panic
Atoi is newer and follows modern conventions
items.explain: The dividing line is who could have prevented it. A string from a user can be anything, so parsing must be able to fail gracefully. An out-of-range index means your own code computed something impossible — continuing would just corrupt state further.
